::: {.callout-note title="Chapter overview"}
This chapter compares means by examining variation. Two invented studies
provide the observations: a one-way experiment on background sound while
studying carries the first analyses, and a two-factor experiment
crossing feedback with practice schedule carries the factorial analysis,
which asks how a comparison changes across practice schedules. We follow
the one-way ANOVA from individual scores to its F distribution,
distinguish its omnibus question from a particular contrast, and explain
how the comparison family determines an interval's coverage. Cell means
and simple effects then reveal what main effects can conceal. A worked
three-way table, set beside the two-way table of the same study, shows
how a third factor adds rows and how a two-way pattern can itself
change, and what a fourth factor would add. By the end, you will be able
to read an ANOVA table and the F distribution behind it, interpret a
contrast and its uncertainty within a family of comparisons, and connect
a factorial pattern to the design and model conditions that support its
interpretation.
:::

Two **invented studies** supply the observations. In the first, thirty
first-year university students each read the same passage for 20
minutes and then answer a 20-item reading-comprehension quiz. Each
student reads in an individual session and is randomly assigned to one
of three background-sound conditions, ten to each: *Silence*,
*Instrumental music*, or *Music with lyrics* playing during the reading.
In the second, twenty-four students study the same fractions material
under one of three kinds of feedback and one of two practice schedules,
four different students in each combination, and take a common 20-item
quiz one week after their final practice. These design details and all
scores are invented for teaching.

Our first question concerns the background-sound study: how do the
three sound-condition means compare? Chapter 3 built, step by step, the
tools for one comparison: an estimate and its standard error, a
confidence interval, a hypothesis test with its p-value, and the t tests
for one sample, paired samples and two independent samples. For two
independent groups sharing one spread, the equal-variance t test pooled
the two group variances. We extend that reasoning to several groups,
keeping the difference between an overall pattern and particular
comparisons visible.

Our later question concerns the feedback-by-practice study: how does
the feedback comparison depend on practice schedule? Section 4 answers
it, and Section 4.7 adds a third factor, the timing of the quiz.

## Comparison Questions and Designs {#sec-ch04-design}

### Outcomes, factors and levels

Both outcomes count correct answers. A comprehension score is the
number of reading-comprehension items answered correctly, and a quiz
score is the number of fractions items answered correctly; each runs
from 0 to 20, and higher values mean more correct answers. A four-point
difference therefore means four more correct answers on average; it
does not by itself describe every aspect of reading comprehension or of
learning fractions.

A **factor** in analysis of variance is a categorical variable defining
groups or conditions. Its categories are **levels**. Background sound is
one factor with three levels, so its analysis is **one-way**. The second
study crosses two factors, feedback with three levels and practice
schedule with two, so its analysis is **two-way** (Section 4). One-way
and two-way refer to the number of factors, not to the number of
levels: a one-way analysis can compare three, four or more groups, and a
third or fourth crossed factor gives a three-way or four-way layout
(Section 4.7). This use of *factor* differs from a latent factor used to
represent shared indicator variation in a measurement model.

`sound` and `score`; students S01--S30 appear ten to each condition in
the order Silence, Instrumental music, Music with lyrics, and Silence is
the reference condition for the comparisons of Section 3.

### Design determines the relevant comparison

Random allocation is stipulated in each invented story. If implemented
in a real study, it could support a causal comparison among the
participating students, subject to adherence, relevant interference and
missing outcomes. It would not make the participants a random sample of
all students, and the data table alone establishes neither the
implementation of assignment nor representativeness.

Different designs can produce superficially similar tables. If students
who heard one sound condition read together in one room, they would
share that session's influences, such as noise from a corridor or a
disruption partway through the reading. If whole classes received
conditions, students within a class would share influences and the
class could be the assignment unit. If each student were measured twice,
the two outcomes would form a pair. For a real study, identify the
allocation, any repeated measurements, shared sessions or classroom
clustering, and any losses before choosing the error term: an
uncertainty formula must reflect these connections rather than treat
every row as an independent assignment.

## One-Way ANOVA {#sec-mean-comparison}

### Grouped observations and the idea of ANOVA

The three sound conditions have means 12, 10 and 8 comprehension points
(@tbl-ch04-group-summary). Each has ten scores, and the sample SDs,
2.7080, 2.4037 and 2.5820, are similar. The ranges overlap widely: some
students who read with lyrics playing, scoring 11 or 12, outscored some
who read in silence, scoring 8 or 9. A difference between means
summarizes group distributions; it does not say that every student in
one group outperformed every student in another.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

| Sound condition | n | Mean | SD | Range |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| Silence | 10 | 12 | 2.7080 | 8--16 |
| Instrumental music | 10 | 10 | 2.4037 | 6--14 |
| Music with lyrics | 10 | 8 | 2.5820 | 4--12 |

: Descriptions of the thirty background-sound scores. {#tbl-ch04-group-summary tbl-colwidths="[36,10,18,18,18]"}

Why not compare the conditions two at a time? Three conditions give
three pairwise differences, and a t test of each at the .05 level asks
three questions. If all three model means were equal, the chance that
at least one of the three tests rejects wrongly would be about .12,
more than twice the .05 that each test states. The three tests are not
independent, because each group mean enters two of them; three
independent tests would give $1-.95^3=.1426$. Chapter 3, Section 7.3,
noted that several tests raise the chance of at least one false
rejection. Analysis of variance therefore asks the overall question
first, in one test at .05: do the three means differ at all? Particular
comparisons follow, declared in advance or calibrated as a family
(Section 3.3).

How can one test compare three means at once?
@fig-ch04-separation-spread draws the thirty scores in its left panel:
each box shows a group's median and middle half, and the points keep
every student visible, which a bar chart of the three means would hide.
The right panel is a constructed version with every score's distance
from its group mean doubled, so the group means and counts stay fixed
while the spread doubles. The same two-point steps between the means
stand out against the narrow spread on the left and are lost in the
wide spread on the right. That is the idea of analysis of variance: it
judges how far apart the group means lie relative to how widely scores
vary within the groups [@cetinkaya2024; @kutner2005]. Section 2.3 turns
this comparison into the F statistic and returns to the right panel with
numbers.

### The group-mean model and the partition of variation

Write $Y_{ij}$ for the random score of student $i$ in sound condition $j$.
Here $j$ indexes a group, rather than a data-file column. The one-way
model is

$$
Y_{ij}=\mu_j+\varepsilon_{ij}.
$$

The unknown $\mu_j$ is the group mean in the model, and
$\varepsilon_{ij}$ is that student's unknown departure from it. After
fitting the group means, the **fitted value** is
$\widehat y_{ij}=\bar y_j$, and the **residual** is
$e_{ij}=y_{ij}-\bar y_j$. A residual is calculated from observed scores
and fitted means; a model error is a departure from an unknown model
mean. This distinction will recur in regression.

The comparison concerns two explanations of the same thirty scores.
A **one-mean model**, $Y_{ij}=\mu+\varepsilon_{ij}$, gives every sound
condition the same mean. The **group-mean model** lets each condition
have its own mean, $Y_{ij}=\mu_j+\varepsilon_{ij}$. Both allow students
to differ around their model mean. The second model can reproduce the
first by setting its three means equal. Fitting separate means can
therefore reduce the residual variation even when the population means
are equal; a smaller residual sum of squares alone cannot settle the
comparison. Section 2.3 judges that improvement relative to the
remaining within-group variation and the two extra mean parameters.

The observed grand mean is $\bar y=10$, the average of the three
group means because the groups are equally sized. Every score's
distance from the grand mean splits into two parts, the group's
departure from the grand mean and the student's residual:

$$
y_{ij}-\bar y=(\bar y_j-\bar y)+(y_{ij}-\bar y_j).
$$

For the Music-with-lyrics student who scored 4, $4-10=(8-10)+(4-8)$:
the group mean lies two points below the grand mean, and this student
another four points below the group mean. The first part is shared by
every student in the group; the second differs from student to
student.

[]{#app-ch04-small-data}Squaring the parts and adding over all thirty
students turns the split into a partition of the total squared
variation, $SS_T=SS_B+SS_W$, where

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_T&=\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}(y_{ij}-\bar y)^2,\\
SS_B&=\sum_{j=1}^Jn_j(\bar y_j-\bar y)^2,\\
SS_W&=\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}(y_{ij}-\bar y_j)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The **total sum of squares** $SS_T$ measures variation around the one
grand mean. The **between-group sum of squares** $SS_B$ counts each
group's departure once for every student in that group, so it grows as
the group means separate. The **within-group sum of squares** $SS_W$
adds the squared residuals around the group means. The partition holds
because, within each group, the cross-products
$2(\bar y_j-\bar y)(y_{ij}-\bar y_j)$ sum to zero: the group's departure
is the same for every student, and the residuals of a group sum to zero.
For the background-sound study, $SS_B=80$, $SS_W=178$ and
$SS_T=258$, in squared comprehension points. The Instrumental-music
group adds nothing to $SS_B$, because its mean equals the grand mean,
although its scores still vary. The partition is arithmetic; it needs no
Normality or independence assumption. Those conditions enter when the
partition is used for inference, in Section 2.3.

### Degrees of freedom, mean squares and the F test {#sec-ch04-f-test}

The F statistic puts the idea of @fig-ch04-separation-spread into one
number, the variation among the group means divided by the variation
within the groups, each measured as an average squared departure. A sum
of squares grows with both the size of the departures and the number of
them, so each is divided by its **degrees of freedom** (df), the number
of departures that can vary freely, before the two sources are compared.
The F statistic has two kinds of df.

- The **between-groups df**, $J-1=2$, are the numerator df. The three
  group means can take any values, but once the grand mean is fixed
  their departures from it, weighted by group size, sum to zero, so
  only two of them are free.
- The **within-groups df**, $N-J=27$, are the denominator df. The ten
  residuals of each group sum to zero, so nine of them are free in each
  group, and three groups give 27.

The two kinds add to the total df, $N-1=29$, because the thirty
departures from the grand mean sum to zero. Dividing each sum of squares
by its df gives a **mean square**,

$$
MS_B=\frac{SS_B}{J-1},\qquad MS_W=\frac{SS_W}{N-J},\qquad
F=\frac{MS_B}{MS_W}.
$$

The within-group mean square is the pooled variance of Chapter 3,
Section 2.2, extended from two groups to $J$: each group's sample
variance $s_j^2$ is weighted by its own df,

$$
MS_W=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^J(n_j-1)s_j^2}{\sum_{j=1}^J(n_j-1)}.
$$

With equal group sizes it is the plain average of the group variances,
here 7.3333, 5.7778 and 6.6667. @tbl-ch04-one-way-anova gathers the
parts.

Allowing the means to differ removes 80 squared score points from the
residual variation, the between-group SS in the ANOVA table, while
using two more mean parameters. Its mean square is 40, compared with
6.5926 left within groups, giving the same F of 6.0674. Thus the
between/within reading and the model-comparison reading explain one
test. The reference distribution asks how large this improvement could
be when one common mean and the stated error conditions hold. It does
not ask whether adding parameters improves the observed fit at all.

Write $\mu_S$, $\mu_I$ and $\mu_L$ for the model means of Silence,
Instrumental music and Music with lyrics. The omnibus null hypothesis is
$H_0:\mu_S=\mu_I=\mu_L$; the alternative says that at least two of these
means differ. Judging whether 6.0674 is large needs the distribution
that the statistic would follow if the null were true.

Three conditions support this reference distribution;
@fig-ch04-model draws the last two. **Independent observations**: one student's
departure from a group mean carries no information about another
student's departure. Here that rests on the design (Section 1.2), with
students individually assigned, each reading in an individual session
and scored once; no display of the scores can establish it.
**Approximately Normal errors**: the departures around each group mean,
not the pooled mixture of all thirty scores, have a roughly Normal
shape. **A common variance**: one error variance $\sigma^2$ describes
every group, which is what allows $MS_W$ to pool the three group
variances. In model shorthand, the errors $\varepsilon_{ij}$ are
independent Normal with mean zero and common variance $\sigma^2$.

Under the null, both mean squares estimate the same error variance, so
their ratio tends to lie near 1; the numerator also grows with the
separation of the model means, so a large ratio is evidence against
equality. Under the three conditions and the null, F follows an
**F distribution**, one of a family of right-skewed distributions on
positive values, each indexed by its two df, numerator first: here
$F(2,27)$. The left panel of @fig-ch04-f-reference shows three members
of the family and marks each one's 5% point, the value beyond which 5%
of the distribution lies. With few denominator df, as in $F(2,8)$, the
error variance is poorly estimated and large ratios occur more often by
chance: its curve looks much like that of $F(2,27)$, but its heavier
tail moves the 5% point from 3.3541 to 4.4590. With more numerator df,
as in $F(5,27)$, the distribution gathers near 1 and its 5% point falls
to 2.5719.

The dark area in the right panel of @fig-ch04-f-reference, .0067, is
read in the same way as the tail areas and p-values of Chapter 3,
Section 4. Only the right tail counts, because greater separation of the
means produces a larger ratio. Under the null and the model conditions,
a ratio at least as large as 6.0674 occurs with that probability. The
observed F lies beyond the critical value 3.3541, so at a prespecified
.05 significance level the equality null is rejected; comparing F with
the critical value and comparing p with .05 give the same decision. This
is evidence about the three-mean pattern, not a probability that the
null is true and not an identification of which particular comparisons
differ.

The box below states, in the four lines used since Chapter 3, what this
F test addresses, what it rests on, what the data can check and what the
result supports.

[]{#ch04-justify-oneway}

::: {.callout-tip title="Justifying the analysis"}
- **Target:** whether the model means of the three sound conditions,
  $\mu_S$, $\mu_I$ and $\mu_L$, are all equal for the thirty students of
  the background-sound study, on the 0--20 comprehension scale; the
  observed means 12, 10 and 8 estimate them.
- **Conditions:**
  - *Secured by design:* individual random assignment, ten students to
    each condition, and one score per student from an individual
    session, so the scores are independent and a difference among the
    means reads as an effect of sound among these students, not in a
    wider population (Sections 1.2 and 2.3).
  - *Model assumptions:* Normal errors with one common variance (Section
    2.3), estimated by $MS_W=6.5926$ on 27 df.
  - *Choices and defaults:* all thirty students, none missing; a .05
    level fixed in advance; the right tail of $F(2,27)$; the classical
    calibration that pools the group variances.
- **Check:** the group SDs, 2.7080, 2.4037 and 2.5820, are similar, the
  largest 1.1266 times the smallest, with ten students in each group,
  and the boxplots show no outlying score; markedly unequal SDs would
  call for Welch's one-way ANOVA, chosen in advance (Section 5.2). Ten
  scores per group say little about shape, and independence rests on
  the design.
- **Bound:** $F(2,27)=6.0674$, $p=.0067$ is evidence at the .05 level
  against equal means for these thirty students under the model. It
  does not say which means differ or by how much (Section 3), and,
  with invented scores, says nothing about real studying.
:::

With equal group sizes $n$, the numerator of F shows directly what the
statistic compares:

$$
F=\frac{n\sum_{j=1}^J(\bar y_j-\bar y)^2/(J-1)}{MS_W}.
$$

Three quantities move it, the same three that moved Chapter 3's t
statistic (Section 4.4): the separation of the group means, the group
size $n$ and the within-group spread in $MS_W$.
@tbl-ch04-what-moves-f changes one of them at a time; its second row is
the right panel of @fig-ch04-separation-spread.

classical one-way F test and Chapter 3's **equal-variance two-sample t
test** (Section 5.3) share one model, one pooled variance and one
residual df, and $F(1,N-2)=t_{N-2}^2$. Chapter 3 labels its two groups 1
and 0; this chapter numbers groups $j=1,\ldots,J$, so its two-group case
uses 1 and 2.

For Silence and Music with lyrics alone, the pooled variance is 7

same two-sided $p=.0033$. Squaring removes direction, so the signed
difference, Silence minus Music with lyrics, 4 points, carries it.

pattern. [Appendix A](#app-ch04-pooled-identity) derives the identity,

Music-with-lyrics-minus-Silence difference is $-4$: two and four
fewer items answered correctly, on average, than in silence. Whether a
difference of this size matters for studying needs a substantive
criterion, not only a p-value. One descriptive summary of the overall
separation is **eta squared**,

$$

$$

divides a difference by a stated SD; dividing it by an individual-score
SD gives a different quantity from dividing it by the SE of that
difference.

## Contrasts and Multiple Comparisons {#sec-ch04-contrasts}

### Contrasts and their weights

The omnibus question asks whether all three model means agree. A
**contrast** states a particular comparison as a weighted combination
of means whose weights sum to zero:

$$
C=\sum_{j=1}^Jc_j\mu_j,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^Jc_j=0,
\qquad \widehat C=\sum_{j=1}^Jc_j\bar y_j.
$$

The symbol $C$ here names a contrast, and $\widehat C$ its estimate.
The weights specify both the comparison and its direction.

The study plan declares two questions, each music condition against
Silence: Instrumental music minus Silence and Music with lyrics minus
Silence. A negative estimate means fewer items answered correctly than
in silence. A broader question compares the equal average of the two
music conditions with Silence. In the declared order Silence,
Instrumental music, Music with lyrics, the three comparisons have these
weights:

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

| Comparison | Weights | Estimate |
|:--|:--|--:|
| Instrumental music minus Silence | $(-1,1,0)$ | $-2$ |
| Music with lyrics minus Silence | $(-1,0,1)$ | $-4$ |
| Equal average of the two music conditions minus Silence | $(-1,1/2,1/2)$ | $-3$ |

: Three contrast meanings in the background-sound study. {#tbl-ch04-weights tbl-colwidths="[55,25,20]"}

Only the first two form the declared family whose intervals Section 3.3
calibrates together. The third gives the two music conditions equal
weight; its $-3$ hides that they fall 2 and 4 points below Silence, so it
does not replace both separate comparisons when both are required. The
weights also fix the scale: weights such as $(-2,1,1)$ double the
estimate and its SE and report twice a mean difference, whereas
$(-1,1/2,1/2)$ keeps the estimate in comprehension points. With unequal
group sizes, equal weights and weights proportional to student counts
answer different questions ([Appendix B.1](#app-ch04-weighting)).

### The standard error of a contrast

The SE of a contrast extends the two-group SE of Chapter 3,
Section 2.2. A difference between two means is the contrast with
weights $+1$ and $-1$, and Chapter 3's pooled SE can be written with
those weights visible:

$$
s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_0}}
=\sqrt{s_p^2\left(\frac{1^2}{n_1}+\frac{(-1)^2}{n_0}\right)}.
$$

Under the independent common-variance model, each estimated group mean
has variance $\sigma^2/n_j$, and the variance of a weighted sum of
independent means uses the **squared weights**. Opposite signs define a
difference; they do not make independent sources of uncertainty cancel.
Several groups make two changes to Chapter 3's form: the weights $c_j$
can describe any comparison, and $s_p^2$ is replaced by $MS_W$, the
variance pooled over all $J$ groups (Section 2.3). Then

$$
\widehat{SE}(\widehat C)=
\sqrt{MS_W\sum_{j=1}^J\frac{c_j^2}{n_j}}.
$$

For each difference with Silence,

$$
\widehat{SE}=
\sqrt{\frac{178}{27}\left(\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{10}\right)}
=1.1483\text{ points}.
$$

Each contrast uses the three-group estimate 6.5926 and its 27 error df,
although it uses only two of the three means: under the common-variance
model all three groups estimate the same $\sigma^2$, so pooling them
uses more information than the two-group refit of Section 2.4, whose
7.0000 on 18 df gives an SE of 1.1832. For the equal-average contrast,
the squared weights $1$, $1/4$ and $1/4$ give $\widehat{SE}=0.9944$.
This smaller SE belongs to a different estimand, an average of two
means compared with the reference; it does not make either separate
comparison more precise. The
[NIST contrast explanation](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/prc/section4/prc436.htm)
develops the same weighted-mean variance calculation.

### Families of comparisons and the familywise error rate {#sec-ch04-families}

Section 2.1 showed that several tests of one study raise the chance of
at least one false rejection, so a reader needs to know how many
comparisons were made and when each was chosen. A **planned
comparison** is declared before the results are seen, as this study's
plan declares each music condition against Silence. A **post hoc
comparison** is chosen after the results are seen, often because it
looks large, such as the largest of the three pairwise differences.
[Chapter 3, Section 7.3](chapter_03.qmd#sec-ch03-selection),
showed that a result chosen because it looks large tends to overstate
its target; the same selection problem arises among the several
comparisons of one study.

Each comparison tested at level .05 has a **per-comparison error rate**,
also called the testwise rate, of .05: when its null hypothesis is true,
it rejects wrongly with probability .05. A reader of the whole report,
however, cares whether any of its comparisons is a false rejection. The
**familywise error rate** is the probability of at least one Type I
error (Chapter 3, Section 7.2) among all the comparisons of a family.
For $m$ independent comparisons whose null hypotheses are all true, each
tested at .05, it is $1-(1-.05)^m$, which @fig-ch04-familywise draws
against $m$: already .1426 for three comparisons and .2262 for five.

To hold the familywise rate at .05, **Bonferroni's method** tests each
of the $m$ comparisons at level $.05/m$, or builds each interval with
confidence $1-.05/m$. Its guarantee needs no independence, because the
probability that at least one of several events occurs is at most the
sum of their probabilities:

$$
P(\text{at least one false rejection})
\le\sum_{k=1}^mP(\text{false rejection }k)
=m\cdot\frac{.05}{m}=.05.
$$

[]{#app-ch04-families}The lower line of @fig-ch04-familywise stays at or
below .05 for every $m$. The price is width: each interval is wider and
each comparison has less power, so a family should contain the
comparisons that matter rather than every comparison that could be
made. Bonferroni's method suits any declared set; other methods are
calibrated for particular families and give narrower intervals when
their family fits the question (@tbl-ch04-families) [@tukey1953;
@kutner2005].

## Multi-Way (Factorial) ANOVA {#sec-ch04-two-way}

Analysis of variance with two or more crossed factors is **multi-way**,
or **factorial**, ANOVA; this section works the two-way case in full
with the feedback-by-practice study and closes, in Section 4.7, with a
worked three-way analysis and the structure of four-way designs.

### The two-way design and what interaction means {#sec-ch04-interaction-idea}

In the feedback-by-practice study, twenty-four students study the same
fractions material and complete a common 20-item quiz one week after
their final practice. *Rereading* offers the worked material again;
*Answer feedback* supplies the correct answer after an attempt;
*Explanatory feedback* supplies the answer with a worked explanation.
*Massed* practice occurs in one session and *Spaced* practice in two
shorter sessions with the same total practice time. Random allocation
places four different students in each combination of feedback and
practice (@tbl-ch04-feedback-scores).

\Needspace{10\baselineskip}

| Feedback condition | Massed practice | Spaced practice |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Rereading | 4, 5, 7, 8 | 4, 5, 7, 8 |
| Answer feedback | 6, 7, 9, 10 | 10, 11, 13, 14 |
| Explanatory feedback | 8, 9, 11, 12 | 16, 17, 19, 20 |

: Invented fractions-quiz scores, four different students per cell, on a 0--20 scale. {#tbl-ch04-feedback-scores tbl-colwidths="[38,31,31]"}

A **cell** contains the cases that share one level of each factor;
Answer feedback with Spaced practice is one cell. Crossing three
feedback levels with two practice levels gives six cells, and four
students in every cell make the layout **balanced**, as ten students
per condition balance the one-way layout. Each score belongs to a
different student, the stipulated assignment and measurement unit: the
four scores of a cell are not repeated measurements, and the Massed and
Spaced scores are not paired. Each cell's scores lie 2 and 1 points
below and above its mean, a repeated pattern that simplifies the
arithmetic; it is a teaching construction, not evidence of Normal
errors, equal variances or an educational effect. The course data file
`feedback_practice.csv` holds the same scores in one row per student,
with columns `student`, `feedback`, `practice` and `score`, ordered by
feedback, then practice, then student.

A two-way ANOVA compares a numerical score across combinations of two
factors. Chapter 3's two-way frequency table (Section 6) instead counts
cases in combinations of two categorical variables: *two-way* describes
a layout, not a shared statistical test.

Two factors **interact** when the effect of one factor differs across
the levels of the other. Here is one invented illustration, outside the
chapter's two studies. Suppose a short vocabulary preview is given
before a reading passage, and that students are also grouped by whether
they began with weak or strong vocabulary. The preview raises
comprehension scores substantially for the students who began weak, and
barely changes them for the students who began strong. The effect of the
preview *depends on* prior vocabulary: that dependence is the
interaction. Describing only an average preview effect would tell a
reader that the preview helps somewhat, and would conceal that it helps
one group a great deal and the other hardly at all.

Studying two factors together in one crossed design has three
advantages over running two separate one-factor studies.

1. **It is more efficient.** Every student contributes to both factor
   comparisons at once, because the levels of one factor are spread
   across the levels of the other. A crossed design therefore needs
   fewer cases per condition than a series of separate one-factor
   studies aimed at the same comparisons.
2. **It reduces residual variation.** A second factor that influences
   the outcome moves variation out of the error term and into the fit.
   Section 4.4 shows what leaving practice out does to these scores.
3. **It makes interaction examinable.** Only a crossed design supports
   the question of whether a comparison changes across the other
   factor's levels. A series of one-factor studies supplies no
   estimate of that change, however carefully each one is run.

Practice schedule therefore gives each feedback comparison a context.
We can compare feedback conditions within Massed practice, within Spaced
practice, or after averaging over the two schedules, and these are
distinct quantities. A **main effect** compares one factor's levels
after averaging across the other factor with stated weights. A
**simple effect** makes the comparison at a specified level of the
other factor. **Interaction** means that a comparison changes across
those levels.

### Additivity and the full model {#sec-ch04-full-model}

If feedback and practice combined additively, every cell mean would be
the grand mean plus its feedback effect plus its practice effect, and
the schedule difference would be the same in every row.
@tbl-ch04-interaction-departures sets these **additive predictions**
beside the observed cell means. The difference between an observed cell
mean and its additive prediction is an **interaction departure**.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

| Cell | Observed mean | Additive prediction | Interaction departure |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Rereading, Massed | 6 | 4 | 2 |
| Rereading, Spaced | 6 | 8 | $-2$ |
| Answer feedback, Massed | 8 | 8 | 0 |
| Answer feedback, Spaced | 12 | 12 | 0 |
| Explanatory feedback, Massed | 10 | 12 | $-2$ |
| Explanatory feedback, Spaced | 18 | 16 | 2 |

: Observed cell means, additive predictions from the grand mean and both effects, and interaction departures. {#tbl-ch04-interaction-departures tbl-colwidths="[37,19,22,22]"}

Answer feedback's two cells sit exactly on their predictions, but the
other four do not: Rereading gains less from spacing than the average,
and Explanatory feedback more, by 2 points in each cell. Agreement in
one row does not make the whole layout additive.

The full mean model includes such departures:

$$
Y_{ijk}=\mu+\alpha_j+\beta_k+(\alpha\beta)_{jk}
        +\varepsilon_{ijk}.
$$

Here $i=1,\ldots,4$ identifies a student within a cell, $j=1,2,3$
identifies feedback and $k=1,2$ identifies practice. The grand model
mean is $\mu$; $\alpha_j$ and $\beta_k$ are the factor effects;
$(\alpha\beta)_{jk}$ is the interaction departure; and
$\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the individual error around the cell mean.
These indexed effects are distinct from the unindexed error
probabilities $\alpha$ and $\beta$ used in hypothesis testing.

In the balanced decomposition, main effects sum to zero, and
interaction departures sum to zero along each row and each column, so
they carry only the pattern left after the two main effects. With two
columns, a row's second departure is the negative of its first, and the
three first-column departures, 2, 0 and $-2$, sum to zero, so only two
of them are free. Thus the interaction has $(3-1)(2-1)=2$ df. It
describes a two-dimensional pattern, rather than one particular
four-cell difference.

[]{#app-ch04-two-way-arithmetic}Each score's distance from the grand
mean now splits into four parts, a feedback effect, a practice effect,
an interaction departure and the student's residual. Squaring the parts
and adding over all 24 students gives, in this balanced layout as in
Section 2.2, four sums of squares with matching df:

$$
SS_T=SS_A+SS_B+SS_{AB}+SS_E,\qquad
df_T=df_A+df_B+df_{AB}+df_E.
$$

In this two-way table A denotes feedback and B practice, so $SS_B$ now
means the practice component, not the between-group component of the
one-way table, and $SS_E$ is the within-cell error:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_A&=2n\sum_j(\bar y_{j\cdot}-\bar y)^2=256,\\
SS_B&=3n\sum_k(\bar y_{\cdot k}-\bar y)^2=96,\\
SS_{AB}&=n\sum_j\sum_k
 (\bar y_{jk}-\bar y_{j\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot k}+\bar y)^2
 =64,\\
SS_E&=\sum_j\sum_k\sum_i(y_{ijk}-\bar y_{jk})^2=60.
\end{aligned}
$$

### Simple effects and a declared interaction contrast

The Answer-feedback schedule comparison, Spaced minus Massed, is a
**simple effect**: $12-8=4$ points. Under the full model its SE is
$\sqrt{(10/3)(1/4+1/4)}=1.291$, and with 18 error df a pointwise 95%
interval is $[1.2877,6.7123]$. The two means come from different
students, so this is an independent-cell calculation, not a paired one.

The study plan also declared one interaction comparison before any
scores were seen: whether spacing helps more under Answer feedback
than under Rereading. In model means the target is

$$
C=(\mu_{A,S}-\mu_{A,M})-(\mu_{R,S}-\mu_{R,M}),
$$

one **difference of differences**, estimated as $(12-8)-(6-6)=4$.
Its four cell means come from different students and carry weights 1,
$-1$, $-1$ and 1, so squaring the weights gives
$\widehat{SE}(\widehat C)=\sqrt{(10/3)(1/4+1/4+1/4+1/4)}=1.8257$.
Declared in advance as the study's one interaction question, the
contrast is a family of one, so its 95% interval uses the ordinary
multiplier $t_{.975;18}=2.1009$ and is $[0.1643,7.8357]$. It excludes
zero: under the model, spacing helps more under Answer feedback than
under Rereading, by between 0.1643 and 7.8357 quiz points. This interval
reads with the [factorial box](#ch04-justify-factorial) of Section 4.4,
with two changes: the target becomes this one contrast of four cell
means, and the choices add its declaration before the scores were seen.

As in Section 3.3, the history of the comparison sets its family. The
interaction test, $F(2,18)=9.6$, $p=.0015$, says that some departure
from additivity exists but not which one, and had this contrast been
picked after inspecting the plot, its interval would need a family that
covers every comparison the plot could have suggested, with a larger
multiplier than 2.1009. Each interval here likewise covers its one
stated comparison, not every simple effect or contrast a reader might
inspect afterward.

### A connected interpretation

Three rules order the reading of a factorial result: plot the cell
means first; examine the interaction before the main effects; and when
an interaction is present, report the cell means and conditional
comparisons, reading each main effect as a stated average. Applied to
this study, the schedule differences are 0, 4 and 8 quiz points for
Rereading, Answer feedback and Explanatory feedback; the interaction
test gives $F(2,18)=9.6$, $p=.0015$, under the stated conditions; and
the declared Answer-versus-Rereading difference of schedule differences
is 4 points, with 95% interval $[0.1643,7.8357]$. The feedback and
practice marginal means summarize explicit equal weights, and the cell
means show what those averages conceal.

These conclusions use the 24 students of the feedback-by-practice study
and 18 error df, whereas the one-way conclusions of Sections 2 and 3
concern the background-sound study. They are analyses of invented data,
not evidence that a teaching method succeeds in a population of
students.

means where a difference of differences combines four, so with the same
students per cell and the same error variance its SE is $\sqrt2$, about
1.4, times as large, and matching the precision of a difference of
differences takes twice as many students per cell. The seven F tests of
a three-factor table, each at .05, also form a family in the sense of

([Appendix B.1](#app-ch04-weighting)), and an empty cell leaves some
interactions without an estimate.

Answer feedback grows between the two timings, and reads the other rows
and cells as description. Twelve cells allow 66 pairwise comparisons and
many more contrasts, so a comparison found by searching them needs a
family that covers the search, as Section 3.3 showed for three groups.

### When spreads differ: Welch's one-way ANOVA {#sec-ch04-welch}

When a common variance is doubtful, **Welch's one-way ANOVA** is the
counterpart of Welch's unequal-variance t test in Chapter 3,
Section 5.4. It keeps each group's own variance instead of pooling them
into $MS_W$, weights each group mean by the precision implied by its own
variance and size, $n_j/s_j^2$, and uses an approximate F reference
whose denominator df are estimated from the group variances
[@welch1951]; with two groups its F is the square of Welch's t.
[]{#ch04-justify-welch}It reads with the
[one-way box](#ch04-justify-oneway) of Section 2.3, with two changes:
the model assumption of one common variance is dropped, so each group
mean needs only a near-Normal sampling distribution, and the calibration
changes with it. For the background-sound study it gives
$F(2,17.9561)=5.5144$, $p=.0136$, beside the classical
$F(2,27)=6.0674$, $p=.0067$: with similar spreads and equal group sizes
the two calibrations lead to the same conclusion at .05, although
Welch's p is about twice as large. Its F is slightly smaller, and its
denominator df fall from 27 to 17.9561 because each weight rests on a
variance estimated from its own ten scores. Welch's
method has the scope of one factor: clustering still needs an analysis
that represents the design, and crossed factors with unequal cell
spreads take each stated contrast's SE from the cells' own variances.

The classical F test applies one pooled variance to every group mean.
Chapter 3, Section 5.4, showed for two groups that a pooled variance
misstates the variance of a small group's mean when spreads differ.
@tbl-ch04-welch-consequence shows what this does with three groups: each
row simulates 50,000 studies of three Normal groups with equal means and
the stated SDs, so every rejection at level .05 rejects a true null.

## Reading Bridge {#sec-ch04-bridge}

Comparing several means extends the estimate-and-SE reasoning of
Chapter 3. ANOVA separates sources of variation to ask an omnibus
question; a contrast states a narrower question and its uncertainty.
Main effects average across factor levels, while cell means and
simple effects show the conditional pattern, and a third factor adds
rows to the table and can change a two-way pattern itself. A joint
interaction test and one declared interaction contrast answer different
questions, and the history of a comparison sets the family its interval
must cover.

The same group-mean model can be written using indicator variables,
as Chapter 6 does in R. A measured baseline can also enter an adjusted
model, called analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), which Chapter 9,
Section 2, develops as regression after Chapters 7--8 develop the
regression mathematics, several controls and standardized
predictions. Baseline adjustment accounts for a measured
source of score variation and compares fitted outcomes at a stated common
baseline value, or averages them over the same stated baseline distribution.
The groups need adequate overlap in those baseline values, often called
common support, for those comparisons to be informed by observations.
Adjustment is not a general cure for confounding or missing outcomes.

**Blocking** makes condition comparisons within groups of similar
units. Chapter 3, Section 2.3, illustrates it with paired schools: in
each of twelve schools one class is assigned to each format, so the
uncertainty follows twelve independent within-school comparisons rather
than 480 students. Sampling strata, which organize selection into a
sample, and allocation blocks, which organize treatment comparisons,
have different roles. The three sound conditions and the
feedback-by-practice cells of this chapter instead contain distinct,
individually assigned students. Repeated measurements and classroom
clustering change the covariance structure and the relevant error term;
the shape of a data table cannot settle these design questions.
Chapters 5--6 now make the statistical foundations executable while
keeping the question, records and interpretation beside each
calculation.

Use this reference to revisit the concepts principally explained here.

| Term and common alternatives | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| Factor (grouping factor) | In ANOVA, a categorical variable defining groups or conditions; its categories are levels. This meaning differs from a latent factor used to model shared indicator variation. |
| Analysis of variance (ANOVA) | A method for studying mean differences through sources of variation. One-way ANOVA uses one grouping factor, and multi-way (factorial) ANOVA uses two or more crossed factors, as two-way and three-way ANOVA do; each factor can have several levels. |
| Fitted value | The value a fitted model assigns to an observed case. In a one-way group-mean model, it is that case's group mean. |
| Residual | An observed outcome minus its fitted value. A residual is calculated from the fitted model; an error is the corresponding unknown departure in the population model. |
| Mean square (MS) | A sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom. In classical ANOVA, the within-group mean square estimates the common error variance under the model's conditions. |
| F statistic (F ratio) | In classical ANOVA, a ratio of the mean square for a tested source to the appropriate error mean square. Its null F reference depends on the model and both degrees of freedom. |
| Omnibus test | A test of one joint null hypothesis about a whole pattern, such as equality of all group means. Rejecting it does not identify which comparisons differ or how large they are. |
| Eta squared | The proportion of total observed variation attributed to a specified source in an ANOVA decomposition. In one-way ANOVA, it is between-group divided by total sum of squares. |
| Contrast (linear contrast) | A weighted combination of means whose weights sum to zero, expressing a specific comparison. The means, weights, and target population determine the quantity compared. |
| Familywise error rate (FWER) | The probability of at least one Type I error among a defined family of tests. Procedures such as Bonferroni allocate the error allowance across that family. |
| Simultaneous confidence intervals | A set of intervals calibrated so that, under their conditions, all of them cover their estimands together at the stated familywise rate; Bonferroni, Tukey, and Dunnett are different calibrations for different families. |
| Cell mean and marginal mean | In a two-factor layout, a cell mean is the mean of the cases sharing one level of each factor; a marginal mean averages the cell means across the levels of the other factor, with stated weights. |
| Main effect | A comparison across one factor's levels averaged over the other factor's levels, using stated weights. It remains an average when the conditional pattern differs across levels. |
| Interaction | A pattern in which a comparison across one factor's levels changes with the other factor's level. A difference of differences expresses one such comparison. |
| Simple effect | A comparison across one factor's levels at a specified level of the other factor. It describes a conditional comparison within the factorial design. |
| Three-way interaction (higher-order interaction) | A pattern in which a two-way interaction changes across the levels of a third factor. Each added factor multiplies the cells and adds interactions, so the highest-order interaction is read first and a few comparisons are declared in advance. |

## Appendix A: Deriving the Matched Pooled-t Identity {.unnumbered #app-ch04-pooled-identity}

[]{#app-ch04-calculations}

Section 2.4 states this identity and its conditions; the derivation
shows where it comes from. For two independent groups, let
$\widehat{\Delta\mu}=\bar y_1-\bar y_2$ and $N=n_1+n_2$. Their grand mean is

$$
\bar y=\frac{n_1\bar y_1+n_2\bar y_2}{N}.
$$

Subtracting it from each group mean gives

$$
\bar y_1-\bar y=\frac{n_2}{N}\widehat{\Delta\mu},
\qquad
\bar y_2-\bar y=-\frac{n_1}{N}\widehat{\Delta\mu}.
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_B
&=n_1\left(\frac{n_2}{N}\widehat{\Delta\mu}\right)^2
  +n_2\left(-\frac{n_1}{N}\widehat{\Delta\mu}\right)^2\\
&=\frac{n_1n_2}{N}\widehat{\Delta\mu}^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

There is one numerator df, so $MS_B=SS_B$. Define the pooled
variance $s_p^2=SS_W/(N-2)$, which is Chapter 3's pooled variance and
equals $MS_W$ when $J=2$. Because
$n_1n_2/N=1/(1/n_1+1/n_2)$,

$$
F=\frac{SS_B}{s_p^2}
=\frac{\widehat{\Delta\mu}^2}{s_p^2(1/n_1+1/n_2)}=t^2,
$$

where $t=\widehat{\Delta\mu}/\{s_p\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_2}\}$ is the
equal-variance t statistic.

The equality is algebraic for these matched definitions; the equal
p-values add the test conditions and a two-sided t alternative. It
connects the one-way F test to the equal-variance t test of Chapter 3,
Section 5.3. The paired-samples t test (Chapter 3, Section 5.2) and
Welch's t test (Chapter 3, Section 5.4) have their own SEs and df, so
this algebra supplies neither; Welch's several-group counterpart is
the Welch one-way ANOVA of Section 5.2.

## Appendix B: Reference Notes on Weights, Effect Sizes and a Shared Reference Mean {.unnumbered #app-ch04-comparisons}

### B.1 Unequal-cell weights {.unnumbered #app-ch04-weighting}

In the chapter's balanced data, equal-cell and student-weighted
marginal means coincide. For unequal cell counts, define them
separately:

$$
\bar y_{j\cdot}^{\text{students}}
=\frac{\sum_kn_{jk}\bar y_{jk}}{\sum_kn_{jk}},
\qquad
\bar y_{j\cdot}^{\text{equal cells}}
=\frac1K\sum_k\bar y_{jk}.
$$

The first describes the mixture of students observed in that
feedback group. The second gives each of the $K$ practice conditions
the same weight. Neither is automatically the right target for
every question.

For an illustration, retain Answer's cell means 8 and 12 but
imagine counts of 2 Massed and 6 Spaced students. The equally
weighted mean is $(8+12)/2=10$; the student-weighted mean is
$(2\times8+6\times12)/8=11$. These are hypothetical weights,
not changes to the actual four-per-cell dataset. A comparison of
feedback groups using different schedule mixtures can combine a
feedback comparison with a weighting difference. Adjusted means in
later chapters make their common profile or averaging distribution
explicit for this reason.

### B.2 Effect-size denominators {.unnumbered #app-ch04-effect-sizes}

Section 2.4 used one omnibus summary, eta squared. Software reports
several related summaries whose denominators differ, so each needs its
name and its denominator before it is interpreted.

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}

| Summary | Formula | Denominator | Value here |
|:--|:--|:--|--:|
| Eta squared, one-way | $SS_B/SS_T$ | All observed variation | .3101 |
| Omega squared, one-way | $\dfrac{SS_B-(J-1)MS_W}{SS_T+MS_W}$ | All observed variation plus one error mean square; the numerator first removes the variation expected from noise | .2525 |
| Eta squared for a factorial term | $SS_{\text{term}}/SS_T$ | All observed variation, including the other factors | Interaction .1345 |
| Partial eta squared | $\dfrac{SS_{\text{term}}}{SS_{\text{term}}+SS_E}$ | The term and the error only | Interaction .5161 |

: Four effect-size summaries and their denominators. {#tbl-ch04-effect-sizes tbl-colwidths="[24,25,37,14]"}

Here $\eta^2=80/258=.3101$, $\omega^2=\{80-2(178/27)\}/(258+178/27)=.2525$,
and the interaction's two summaries are $64/476=.1345$ and
$64/(64+60)=.5161$. Omega squared subtracts the between-group
variation that group means show even when the model means are equal;
it rests on the common-variance model, can fall below zero in a small
sample, and like eta squared says nothing about causation. The two
factorial rows show why the name matters: the same interaction is
.5161 of its partial denominator but .1345 of all the variation,
because the partial version leaves the feedback and practice
components out. In one-way ANOVA the two eta squared versions agree,
since the total holds only the factor and error. The raw mean
differences remain necessary for understanding the outcome scale.

### B.3 Two comparisons that share a reference mean {.unnumbered #app-ch04-dependence}

The two declared comparisons of Section 3.3, Instrumental music minus
Silence and Music with lyrics minus Silence, both subtract the Silence
mean, so their estimates are positively related: a Silence mean that
happens to fall high lowers both differences together, and their
covariance under independent group means is
$\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_S)=\sigma^2/10$. The union bound needs no
independence, so the joint coverage of at least 95% stands; it
describes repeated use of the whole procedure, not a probability
assigned to the two realized intervals. Dunnett's method, calibrated
for exactly this family of comparisons with one reference, would give
slightly narrower intervals; Bonferroni's arithmetic is the more
transparent. The
[NIST Bonferroni reference](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/prc/section4/prc473.htm)
explains the joint-coverage bound.
